title: Ideal gases
summary: An [[ideal-gas|ideal gas]] is a model: tiny particles in random motion that never attract each other and bounce off without losing energy. Real gases follow it closely, except at high pressure and low [[temperature|temperature]]. The model gives one equation, $PV = nRT$, linking pressure, volume, temperature and amount.

goals.text: Recognize the four assumptions of the ideal gas model.
Explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour, and why some deviate more than others.
Describe and interpret graphs linking pressure, volume and temperature for a fixed amount of gas.
Use the [[molar-volume|molar volume]] of a gas at STP to convert between amount and volume.
Solve problems with $PV = nRT$ and the combined gas law in SI units, including finding a [[molar-mass|molar mass]].

before.prompt: Convert body temperature, $\pu{37 \degree C}$, to [[kelvin|kelvin]]. Give your answer to the nearest kelvin.
before.hint: Add the same number you add for any Celsius temperature.
before.explain: $T = 37 + 273.15 = \pu{310.15 K}$, which is $\pu{310 K}$ to the nearest kelvin. Revise it in {{lesson:1.1}}.

before.prompt: How many [[mole|moles]] of molecules are in $\pu{7.10 g}$ of chlorine, $\ce{Cl2}$? Give 3 significant figures.
before.hint: Find the [[molar-mass|molar mass]] from the $A_\text{r}$ of chlorine, then use $n = \frac{m}{M}$.
before.explain: $M = 2 \times 35.45 = \pu{70.90 g mol-1}$, so $n = \frac{7.10}{70.90} \approx 0.100$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.6}}.

before.prompt: Two flasks at the same temperature and pressure hold equal volumes of hydrogen and of carbon dioxide. What does [[avogadros-law|Avogadro's law]] say about them?
before.hint: The law is about the number of particles, not their mass or size.

options.text: They contain equal numbers of molecules.
They contain equal masses of gas.
The carbon dioxide flask contains more molecules, because they are heavier.
The hydrogen flask contains more molecules, because they are smaller.

before.explain: Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of particles, whatever the gas. Revise it in {{lesson:1.8}}.

verify.truth: They contain equal numbers of molecules.

blocks.text: A gas is mostly empty space: in air, the molecules fill well under 1% of the volume. The [[kinetic-molecular-theory|kinetic molecular theory]] pictures them flying in straight lines until they hit each other or a wall.

blocks.statement: A model gas whose particles are in constant random motion, have negligible volume, exert no intermolecular forces on each other, and collide elastically.
blocks.plain: Tiny dots that whizz about, never pull on or push each other, and bounce off without losing energy.

blocks.text: The model makes four assumptions about the particles.
1. They move constantly and randomly, in straight lines between collisions.
2. Their own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the container.
3. There are no intermolecular forces between them: no attractions and no repulsions.
4. All their collisions are elastic: the total kinetic energy is the same after a collision as before it.
Gas pressure comes from collisions with the walls. More frequent or harder hits mean a higher pressure.

blocks.question: Outline the assumptions the ideal gas model makes about the particles of a gas.
steps: "Outline" wants a brief account of each point: one assumption per sentence, covering motion, size, forces and collisions.
blocks.answer: The particles are in constant, random motion. The volume of the particles is negligible compared with the volume of the container. There are no intermolecular forces between the particles. All collisions are elastic, so no kinetic energy is lost.

verify.truth: random motion; negligible particle volume; no intermolecular forces; elastic collisions
requires: volume of the particles is negligible

blocks.question: A sealed steel cylinder of argon is left in the sun and warms up. Its volume can't change. Explain, using the ideal gas model, why the pressure inside rises.
steps: A higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy, so the atoms move faster.
Faster atoms hit the walls more often and with more force.
Pressure comes from these hits, and the volume is fixed.
blocks.answer: The higher temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the argon atoms, so they move faster. They hit the walls more often and with more force. Pressure is caused by these collisions with the walls, and the volume is fixed, so the pressure increases.

verify.truth: higher average kinetic energy; faster atoms collide with walls more often and harder

blocks.text: Saying that gas particles get bigger when heated. They move faster; their size doesn't change.

blocks.prompt: Which statement is not an assumption of the ideal gas model?
blocks.hint: Look for the statement that gives the particles a force on each other.

options.text: The particles attract each other weakly when they are close.
The particles move randomly in straight lines between collisions.
The volume of the particles is negligible compared with the container.
Collisions between the particles are elastic.

blocks.explain: An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces at all, not even weak ones.

verify.truth: The particles attract each other weakly when they are close.

blocks.prompt: Two gas particles collide elastically. What does "elastically" mean here?
blocks.hint: It is about the total energy of the pair, not each particle on its own.

options.text: The total kinetic energy of the two particles is unchanged.
Each particle keeps exactly the same speed.
The particles stick together for a moment.
Some kinetic energy is lost as heat.

blocks.explain: Kinetic energy can pass from one particle to the other, so their speeds can change. Only the total stays the same.

verify.truth: The total kinetic energy of the two particles is unchanged.

blocks.text: Real gas particles do take up some space, and they attract each other through [[intermolecular-force|intermolecular forces]]. Under everyday conditions both effects are tiny, so real gases behave almost ideally.

blocks.statement: Real gases deviate most from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature. They are closest to ideal at low pressure and high temperature.
blocks.why: High pressure packs the particles close, so their own volume matters. Low temperature slows them down, so attractions between them take hold.

blocks.text: At very high pressure, the particles are squeezed close together. Their own volume becomes a real fraction of the container, so the gas takes up more space than predicted.
At low temperature, the particles move slowly, so their attractions pull them together as they pass. They hit the walls less often and less hard, so the volume (or pressure) is less than predicted.
Under the same conditions, the stronger the attractions between the particles, the bigger the deviation.

Helium and hydrogen, with very weak [[london-dispersion-force|London (dispersion) forces]], are almost ideal. Among molecules of similar size, those that form [[hydrogen-bond|hydrogen bonds]], such as $\ce{NH3}$ and $\ce{H2O}$, deviate most. Larger molecules deviate more too: they have more electrons and take up more space.

blocks.question: Nitrogen in a storage cylinder is held at about $\pu{20 000 kPa}$. Explain why, at this pressure, its volume is larger than the ideal gas model predicts.
steps: Name the condition and what it does: the molecules are pushed very close together.
Name the assumption that fails, then the effect on the volume.
blocks.answer: At very high pressure the nitrogen molecules are pushed close together. The volume of the molecules themselves is then no longer negligible compared with the volume of the container. So the gas occupies a larger volume than the ideal gas model predicts.

verify.truth: molecules close together, so their own volume is not negligible; volume larger than predicted

blocks.question: At $\pu{250 K}$ and $\pu{100 kPa}$, ammonia deviates from ideal behaviour more than methane. Both molecules have 10 electrons. Explain why.
steps: Equal electron numbers mean similar London forces, so look for another force.
Ammonia has H bonded to N, a highly electronegative atom with a lone pair, so it forms hydrogen bonds. Methane, with H on C, cannot.
Link stronger attractions to the model's assumption of no intermolecular forces.
blocks.answer: Both molecules have 10 electrons, so their London forces are similar. Ammonia molecules also form hydrogen bonds, because hydrogen is bonded to nitrogen, a highly electronegative atom with a lone pair. So the attractions between ammonia molecules are stronger, and it moves further from the ideal model, which assumes no intermolecular forces.

verify.truth: ammonia has hydrogen bonding as well as London forces, so stronger attractions

blocks.prompt: Which gas, under which conditions, behaves most like an ideal gas?
blocks.hint: You want weak attractions, a low pressure and a high temperature all at once.

options.text: helium at 500 K and 50 kPa
helium at 50 K and 5000 kPa
sulfur dioxide at 500 K and 50 kPa
sulfur dioxide at 300 K and 200 kPa

blocks.explain: Helium has very weak London forces and tiny atoms, and low pressure with high temperature shrinks those effects further. Under the same conditions, polar sulfur dioxide, with stronger intermolecular forces, deviates more.

blocks.prompt: At very high pressure, a real gas takes up more volume than the ideal gas model predicts. Which assumption has broken down?
blocks.hint: Which effect would make the volume bigger rather than smaller?

options.text: The particles have negligible volume.
There are no intermolecular forces.
Collisions are elastic.
The particles move randomly.

blocks.explain: Squeezed close, the particles' own volume is no longer negligible. Attractions would make the volume smaller, not larger.

blocks.text: For a fixed amount of gas, hold one of pressure ($P$), volume ($V$) and temperature ($T$) constant and change another: the third responds. You don't need the gas laws' names.
At constant temperature, halve the volume and the particles hit the walls twice as often, so the pressure doubles. Pressure is inversely proportional to volume, and $PV$ stays constant.
At constant pressure, heated particles hit harder, so the gas expands to keep the pressure the same. Volume is directly proportional to temperature.
At constant volume, heated particles hit the walls more often and harder. Pressure is directly proportional to temperature.

blocks.statement: For a fixed amount of ideal gas: at constant $T$, $P \propto \frac{1}{V}$; at constant $P$, $V \propto T$; at constant $V$, $P \propto T$. Here $T$ must be in kelvin.
blocks.why: Kelvin starts at absolute zero, so only kelvin temperatures are proportional to the particles' average kinetic energy.

blocks.alt: Four graphs for a fixed amount of ideal gas. Top left, at constant temperature: pressure against volume is a curve that falls steeply and then levels off, never touching either axis. Top right, at constant temperature: pressure against one over volume is a straight line through the origin. Bottom left, at constant pressure: volume against temperature in kelvin is a straight line through the origin. Bottom right, at constant pressure: volume against temperature in degrees Celsius is a straight line that cuts the volume axis above zero at 0 degrees Celsius; extended backwards as a dashed line, it meets the temperature axis at minus 273 degrees Celsius.
blocks.caption: Lines through the origin need $\frac{1}{V}$, or $T$ in kelvin, on the axis. $PV$ against $P$ at constant temperature is horizontal.

blocks.text: [[avogadros-law|Avogadro's law]] says equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of particles. So one mole of any ideal gas fills the same volume under given conditions.

blocks.statement: The volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at a stated temperature and pressure, symbol $V_\text{m}$.
blocks.plain: How much room one mole of gas takes up under given conditions.

blocks.text: The [[molar-volume|molar volume]] is a constant only once the temperature and pressure are fixed. At [[standard-temperature-and-pressure|standard temperature and pressure]] (STP: $\pu{273.15 K}$ and $\pu{100 kPa}$, data booklet section 4), $V_\text{m} = \pu{22.7 dm3 mol-1}$ (data booklet section 2).

blocks.question: Calculate the volume, in $\pu{dm3}$, occupied by $\pu{3.20 g}$ of methane, $\ce{CH4}$, at STP.
steps: Molar mass: $M = 12.01 + 4(1.01) = \pu{16.05 g mol-1}$ (data booklet section 7).
Amount: $n = \frac{3.20}{16.05} = \pu{0.19938 mol}$. Keep the unrounded value.
Volume: $V = nV_\text{m} = 0.19938 \times 22.7 = \pu{4.526 dm3}$, which is $\pu{4.53 dm3}$ to 3 significant figures.

blocks.question: A student plots the volume of a fixed amount of gas, at constant pressure, against its temperature in $\pu{\degree C}$. Describe the graph and explain why it does not pass through the origin.
steps: Describe the shape: a straight line with a positive gradient.
Volume is proportional to temperature in kelvin, and $\pu{0 \degree C}$ is $\pu{273.15 K}$, so the gas still has a volume there.
blocks.answer: The graph is a straight line with a positive gradient. Volume is directly proportional to the temperature in kelvin, not in degrees Celsius. At $\pu{0 \degree C}$ the gas is at $\pu{273.15 K}$, so the line cuts the volume axis above zero. Extended back, it meets the temperature axis at absolute zero, $\pu{-273.15 \degree C}$.

verify.truth: straight line; V proportional to T in kelvin; extrapolates to absolute zero at -273.15 degrees Celsius
forbids: proportional to the temperature in degrees Celsius

blocks.text: STP ($\pu{273.15 K}$) is not the $\pu{298.15 K}$ standard state used for enthalpy data. At $\pu{298 K}$ and $\pu{100 kPa}$ the molar volume is about $\pu{24.8 dm3 mol-1}$, so check the temperature.

blocks.prompt: A fixed amount of gas is kept at constant temperature, and its pressure is tripled. What happens to its volume?

options.text: It falls to one third of its value.
It falls by one third.
It triples.
It stays the same.

blocks.explain: If $P$ becomes $3P$, $V$ must become $\frac{V}{3}$ to keep $PV$ the same. "Falls by one third" would leave two thirds.

verify.truth: It falls to one third of its value.

blocks.prompt: For a fixed amount of ideal gas, which plot is a straight line through the origin?
blocks.hint: Proportional quantities give a line through the origin.

options.text: pressure against one over volume, at constant temperature
pressure against volume, at constant temperature
volume against temperature in Celsius, at constant pressure
pressure times volume against pressure, at constant temperature

blocks.explain: $P \propto \frac{1}{V}$ at constant temperature. $P$ against $V$ is a curve, the Celsius line misses the origin, and $PV$ against $P$ is horizontal.

verify.truth: pressure against one over volume, at constant temperature

blocks.prompt: What amount, in mol, of nitrogen is in a $\pu{5.00 dm3}$ flask at STP? Give 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Divide the volume by the molar volume at STP.

blocks.text: The three relationships and Avogadro's law combine into one: $PV$ is proportional to $nT$. The constant is the [[gas-constant|gas constant]], $R$.

blocks.statement: The constant $R$ in the ideal gas equation, $\pu{8.31 J K-1 mol-1}$.
blocks.plain: The number that links pressure times volume to amount times temperature.

blocks.text: The equation and $R$ are in the data booklet (sections 1 and 2). With $R = \pu{8.31 J K-1 mol-1}$, use SI units only: $P$ in Pa, $V$ in $\pu{m3}$, $T$ in K and $n$ in mol.
Conversions (data booklet section 4): $\pu{1 kPa} = \pu{1000 Pa}$; $\pu{1 dm3} = \pu{1e-3 m3}$; $\pu{1 cm3} = \pu{1e-6 m3}$; $T(\text{K}) = t(\pu{\degree C}) + 273.15$.
Since $n = \frac{m}{M}$, the equation can also give a molar mass from measured data: $M = \frac{mRT}{PV}$.

blocks.question: A student vaporises a volatile hydrocarbon in a heated gas syringe. $\pu{0.250 g}$ of vapour fills $\pu{86.7 cm3}$ at $\pu{90 \degree C}$ and $\pu{101 kPa}$. Determine the molar mass of the hydrocarbon.
steps: Combine $PV = nRT$ with $n = \frac{m}{M}$: $M = \frac{mRT}{PV}$.
Substitute: $M = \frac{0.250 \times 8.31 \times 363.15}{(1.01 \times 10^{5}) \times (86.7 \times 10^{-6})} = \pu{86.16 g mol-1}$.
The mass was in grams, so $M$ comes out in $\pu{g mol-1}$. An empirical formula of $\ce{C3H7}$ ($43.10$) would make this $\ce{C6H14}$, hexane.

blocks.text: For a fixed amount of gas, $\frac{PV}{T} = nR$ stays constant when the conditions change. That gives the combined gas law.
The units of $P$ and $V$ cancel here, so any unit works if both sides match. Temperature must still be in kelvin.

blocks.question: A weather balloon is filled with $\pu{12.0 m3}$ of helium at $\pu{101 kPa}$ and $\pu{18 \degree C}$. It rises to a height where the pressure is $\pu{27.5 kPa}$ and the temperature is $\pu{-45 \degree C}$. Calculate the new volume of the balloon.
steps: Rearrange: $V_2 = \frac{P_1 V_1 T_2}{T_1 P_2}$. Both pressures are in kPa, so they cancel.
Substitute: $V_2 = \frac{101 \times 12.0 \times 228.15}{291.15 \times 27.5} = \pu{34.54 m3}$.
Sense check: the pressure falls a lot, so the balloon grows.

blocks.prompt: A $\pu{0.750 dm3}$ flask holds a gas at $\pu{22 \degree C}$ and $\pu{135 kPa}$. Calculate the amount of gas, in mol, to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: $n = \frac{PV}{RT}$, with $P$ in Pa, $V$ in $\pu{m3}$ and $T$ in K.

blocks.prompt: A sealed, rigid can holds gas at $\pu{23 \degree C}$ and $\pu{100 kPa}$. It is heated to $\pu{135 \degree C}$. Calculate the new pressure, in kPa, to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: The volume doesn't change, so $\frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}$. Use kelvin.
blocks.explain: $P_2 = \frac{100 \times 408.15}{296.15} \approx \pu{138 kPa}$. Using Celsius gives about $\pu{587 kPa}$, far too high.

blocks.text: Ideal gas: particles in random motion, negligible particle volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions.
Real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature. Under the same conditions, stronger intermolecular forces mean bigger deviations.
Fixed amount of gas: $P \propto \frac{1}{V}$ at constant $T$; $V \propto T$ at constant $P$; $P \propto T$ at constant $V$, with $T$ in kelvin.
Molar volume at STP ($\pu{273.15 K}$, $\pu{100 kPa}$): $V_\text{m} = \pu{22.7 dm3 mol-1}$, so $n = \frac{V}{V_\text{m}}$.
In $PV = nRT$ use SI units: Pa, $\pu{m3}$, K and mol, with $R = \pu{8.31 J K-1 mol-1}$.

mistakes: Using Celsius in a gas calculation. Add $273.15$ first: $\pu{0 \degree C}$ is $\pu{273.15 K}$, not zero.
Mixing units in $PV = nRT$ with $R = 8.31$, such as kPa with $\pu{m3}$ or Pa with $\pu{dm3}$. The answer is out by a factor of 1000, so convert to Pa and $\pu{m3}$ first.
Using $\pu{22.7 dm3 mol-1}$ when the gas is not at STP. Use $PV = nRT$ instead.
Saying real gases deviate most at high temperature. Faster particles feel attractions less: deviation is greatest at low temperature and high pressure.
examTips: "Explain" a deviation: name the condition, then the assumption that fails. High pressure: particle volume is not negligible. Low temperature: intermolecular forces are significant.
"Calculate" with $PV = nRT$: show each conversion to Pa, $\pu{m3}$ and K, the substitution, then the answer to 3 significant figures with its unit.
In Paper 1A graph questions, read the axes first: kelvin or Celsius, $V$ or $\frac{1}{V}$.
